purpose: Conditional decision path for a customer specifying a staircase. Never asks the customer to hold professional vocabulary. Every question offers plain English + 'I'm not sure'. Never calculates measurements, never quotes final price, never claims compliance.
handoff_rule: At any point the customer selects 'I'm not sure' + does not respond to visual comparison, or picks a value flagged 'specialist_review_required', the wizard exits to a professional review request.

Q1_country.question_en: Which country will your staircase be installed in?

Q2_use.question_en: Where in the building will the staircase go?
Q2_use.explanation_en: Different areas have different rules and different typical layouts.

options.label: Hallway - Ground Floor to First Floor
options.help_en: The main staircase connecting your entrance level to the first upper floor. It's the everyday, most-used staircase in the home, so it drives the strongest requirements around headroom, tread depth, handrail height and pitch. The design also sets the visual tone for the whole hallway.

options.label: Second Staircase - First Floor to Second Floor
options.help_en: A staircase between two upper floors — usually the first to a second floor or loft-conversion level. Similar regulations to the main staircase, but layouts are often more constrained by existing walls, ceilings and roof lines, which can influence the shape (winder, quarter-turn, space-saver, etc).

options.label: Loft or attic access only
options.help_en: A dedicated staircase serving a single loft or attic room. Often steeper and narrower than a main staircase — space-saver, paddle-tread and alternating-tread designs are common. Different regulations can apply because it serves one habitable room rather than a whole floor.

options.label: Commercial or public building
options.help_en: A staircase inside a shop, office, hotel, restaurant, school or any other non-domestic building open to the public or staff. Stricter regulations apply around fire escape, width, handrails on both sides, disability access, non-slip surfaces and material fire-ratings. A specialist will review your project before quoting.

options.label: Outdoor / garden
options.help_en: A staircase exposed to the weather — garden steps, deck stairs, balcony or terrace access. Materials, fixings and finishes have to cope with rain, frost, UV and thermal movement. Slip resistance and drainage become primary design drivers, and separate rules can apply depending on where the stair sits.

options.label: Industrial or service access
options.help_en: A staircase in a factory, warehouse, plant room, mezzanine or service access route. Load ratings, non-slip metal treads, kickplates and specific industrial safety codes apply, and pitch allowances differ from domestic stairs. A specialist will review your project before quoting.

Q3_geometry.question_en: What shape of staircase are you thinking of?
Q3_geometry.explanation_en: The shape describes how the staircase turns through your space. If you're not sure, we'll show you the differences visually.

options.label: U-shape — two flights meeting a landing
Winder — wedge-shaped treads at a corner instead of a landing
Spiral — winding around a central column
Helical — smooth spiral around an open central well, no column
Curved — a smooth radius, not a full spiral
Split / imperial — grand staircase that splits at a mid-landing
Paddle / space-saver — alternating half-treads (loft use only in most countries)
I'm not sure — show me the differences

Q4_material_family.question_en: What material family are you thinking about?
Q4_material_family.explanation_en: This is the overall material — you can combine materials later (for example wooden treads with a glass balustrade).

options.label: Glass (usually combined with metal or timber)
I'm not sure — show me options

Q5_structural.question_en: What's the main design of your staircase?
Q5_structural.explanation_en: The main design defines how the staircase looks from the side and underneath. If you're not sure, we can show you the differences side-by-side.

options.label: Closed string staircase
options.help_en: Staircase can sit against a wall on the left or on the right side, in between walls, or free-standing in the centre of a room.

options.label: Cut String staircase One Side
options.help_en: One side sits against a wall (closed wall string); the other, open side has a stepped stringer with the tread ends visible. A traditional decorative style — very common in Victorian and Georgian UK homes.

options.label: Double side Cut String staircase
options.help_en: Both sides have stepped cut stringers with the tread ends visible from either side. Usually installed as a freestanding feature staircase in the middle of a room, not against a wall.

options.label: Mono staircase
options.help_en: A single central steel or timber beam runs underneath the treads, so the staircase appears to sit on a spine with the tread ends floating on either side. A contemporary look — structural engineering is required and the specialist will confirm the beam size for your span.

options.label: Cantilever staircase
options.help_en: Each tread projects out of a load-bearing wall with no visible support underneath — a true floating look. Needs a strong structural wall to carry the loads; the specialist confirms suitability at site visit and specifies the fixings. The most contemporary of the design options.

options.label: Bolt wall staircase
options.help_en: The treads connect to each other and to a wall using bolts — no side stringers. Known as a Bolzentreppe in German-speaking markets where it's very common; less traditional in the UK but growing. Very lightweight visual, mid-way between mono-stringer and cantilever in style.

options.label: I'm not sure — show me the differences

Q5b_central_column.question_en: For your spiral, what is the central column made from?
Q5b_central_column.explanation_en: Spirals are supported by a central column. Steel is most common, but timber and stainless are both available.

Q5c_helical_structure.question_en: For your helical, is there a preference for how the underside looks?
Q5c_helical_structure.explanation_en: Helical staircases hide their structure inside curved stringers. Some are mono-stringer, some are twin-stringer.

options.label: Concealed structure — treads appear to float
I'm not sure — specialist will advise

Q6_riser.question_en: Between the treads — do you want a solid board or an open gap?
Q6_riser.explanation_en: Closed risers give a traditional look and more sound insulation. Open risers give a more contemporary look and let more light through. In some countries the size of the opening is regulated.

options.label: Closed riser — solid board between treads
Open riser — no board between treads
Partial or feature riser — a bar or slats
I'm not sure — show me both

Q7_tread_material.question_en: What material would you like the treads to be?
Q7_tread_material.explanation_en: The treads are what you step on. We ask this separately from the overall material because you can have (for example) timber treads on a metal frame.

options.label: Engineered timber (real wood surface on a stable core)
Timber tread with a carpet runner down the middle
I'm not sure — show me options

Q7a_timber_species.explanation_en: The most popular species vary by country. We show you what's common where you are, plus the international favourites.

Q8_balustrade_material.question_en: What kind of balustrade would you like?
Q8_balustrade_material.explanation_en: The balustrade is the safety barrier on the open side of the staircase. It can be traditional timber, contemporary metal, glass, cable — or a combination.

options.label: Traditional metal (painted mild steel, wrought iron style)
Frameless glass (structural glass in a channel)
Combination — I'll describe with the specialist
I'm not sure — show me the options

Q_handrail_position.question_en: Which side will the handrail be on?
Q_handrail_position.explanation_en: This depends on where the staircase sits in your home. Against a wall on one side means the handrail goes on the other side. A staircase in the middle of a room usually needs handrails on both sides.

options.label: Right side only
options.help_en: The staircase sits against a wall on the left, so the handrail runs down the right (open) side. This is the most common configuration in UK homes.

options.label: Left side only
options.help_en: The staircase sits against a wall on the right, so the handrail runs down the left (open) side.

options.label: Both sides (freestanding staircase)
options.help_en: The staircase stands freely in the middle of a room, away from walls on either side. Both open sides need a handrail. Common in loft conversions, open-plan spaces and architectural feature staircases.

options.label: I'm not sure — a specialist will confirm at site visit

Q9_handrail_material.question_en: What material would you like the handrail to be?
Q9_handrail_material.explanation_en: The handrail is the graspable top rail. It can match the balustrade or be a different material (a common choice is oak handrail on a stainless balustrade).

options.label: Glass cap (on top of glass balustrade — regional)
I'm not sure — match to balustrade

Q10_newel.explanation_en: Newels are the vertical posts at the start, corners and top of the staircase. Style is mostly a look choice (turned, square, box, contemporary).

options.label: Box newel (large square, often for grand stairs)
Hidden — I don't want visible newels (glass or cantilever)

Q11_landing.question_en: Are there landings in the staircase?
Q11_landing.explanation_en: Landings are the level platforms between flights. Your geometry choice already tells us where landings usually go — this is a chance to confirm or adjust.

options.label: Yes — matches the shape I picked
Yes — plus an open landing / balcony at the top
No landings — use winders instead where the stair turns
I'm not sure — let the specialist decide based on site measurement

Q12_finish.question_en: How would you like the timber to be finished?
Q12_finish.explanation_en: The finish is what the wood looks and feels like on the surface. Oil is natural feel, lacquer is harder-wearing, stain changes the colour.

options.label: Hard wax oil (blend of oil + wax)
Painted (colour on riser or tread edge)
Recommend a finish for this look

Q13_extras.explanation_en: Optional features — pick any that apply.

options.label: Integrated lighting (LED strip under tread / step-lights)
Ready for a child safety gate

Q_property_type.question_en: What type of property is this?
Q_property_type.explanation_en: This tells the specialist how the project fits into the wider build — a new build, an existing property, an extension or a conversion have different practical requirements.

options.label: New build
options.help_en: A brand-new house or building currently being constructed from the ground up. The staircase specification usually needs to line up with the build programme (structural, plastering, second fix).

options.label: Existing property / renovation
options.help_en: An existing house or building where the staircase is being replaced, upgraded, or refitted as part of a renovation.

options.label: Extension
options.help_en: An extension being added to an existing property. There may or may not be a new staircase involved — the specialist will confirm.

options.label: Conversion
options.help_en: A loft, garage, basement, barn or other space being converted into habitable rooms. Conversions often need a new staircase to serve the new floor level.

options.label: Commercial / other
options.help_en: A shop, office, hotel, restaurant, school, public building or other non-domestic project. A specialist will review the project scope and applicable regulations before quoting.

Q_build_stage.question_en: Where are you in the build?
Q_build_stage.explanation_en: This helps the specialist understand the timing — a project at planning stage is very different from one where plastering is already complete.

options.label: Just looking for a quotation at this stage

Q_replace_existing.question_en: Is the existing staircase being replaced?
Q_replace_existing.explanation_en: Whether you're swapping out an existing staircase or adding one where none exists changes what the specialist needs to plan for.

options.label: New staircase where there isn't currently one

Q_opening_ready.question_en: Is the staircase opening already prepared?
Q_opening_ready.explanation_en: The 'opening' is the hole in the upper floor that the staircase rises into. Whether it's already framed and ready — or still to be built — affects lead time.

options.label: Yes — ready for the staircase
options.help_en: The opening is fully framed and dimensioned, and the staircase can be installed as soon as it's manufactured.

options.label: No — still being constructed
options.help_en: The opening is being built or altered. The specialist will co-ordinate final dimensions with the site.

options.label: Not yet — no opening yet
options.help_en: There's no opening yet. The specialist will help agree the position and dimensions before manufacture.

Q_customer_type.explanation_en: This helps the specialist route your enquiry appropriately — private homeowners and trade customers are handled slightly differently.

Q_vat_status.explanation_en: Useful for the specialist to know for commercial enquiries. NEX doesn't calculate VAT treatment — the specialist confirms this in the quotation.

Q_install_required.question_en: Do you need supply only, or supply and installation?
Q_install_required.explanation_en: Some customers want the staircase manufactured and delivered only. Others want the specialist to install it on site.

options.label: Supply and installation
options.help_en: The specialist manufactures, delivers and installs the staircase.

options.label: Supply only
options.help_en: The specialist manufactures and delivers the staircase. You (or your own contractor) install it on site.

Q_supply_market.question_en: Where is the staircase being supplied?
Q_supply_market.explanation_en: Local projects and export projects are handled differently — export doesn't necessarily mean the specialist installs on site.

options.label: For a project in my country

Q_export_country.question_en: Which country will the staircase be supplied to?
Q_export_country.explanation_en: This helps the specialist plan shipping, packaging and any country-specific compliance needs.

Q_project_stage.question_en: Where are you in the buying journey?
Q_project_stage.explanation_en: This tells the specialist how to prioritise your enquiry — an early-quote request is very different from a ready-to-proceed order.

options.label: Just exploring / obtaining an early quotation

Q_attachments_info.body_en: You'll be able to attach photos, sketches, dimension drawings and inspiration images in the follow-up chat with your specialist. Nothing to attach here — it happens naturally once you send this specification through.

Q_notes.question_en: Anything else the specialist should know?
Q_notes.explanation_en: Optional — write anything that would help the specialist quote your project accurately. Site access, deadlines, budget range, existing staircase issues, style references, or anything else.
Q_notes.placeholder_en: e.g. we're aiming for a contemporary look but with warm oak tones, and we need the staircase installed before Christmas…

Q14_summary.question_en: Here's your specification — anything to adjust before we pass it to a specialist for a professional review?

actions.label: Send to specialist for a quote
Save my choices — I'm not ready yet

handoff_professional.message_en: Thanks — a specialist will review your choices, take site measurements, confirm regulations for your region and give you a full quote. Nothing about your specification is calculated by NEX — every measurement, structural detail and price comes from the professional.
